name: Bystander effect
statement: A person is less likely to help someone in trouble, and slower to act, as the number of other witnesses grows.
meaning: The claim is about one witness, not about the crowd. Darley and Latané argued that a lone bystander carries the whole pressure to act, while several bystanders share it, so the responsibility felt by any one of them falls. Two further mechanisms travel with it. Blame for doing nothing is also divided, and a witness who cannot see the others can tell himself that somebody has already called for help. None of this requires the witness to be indifferent. The 1968 paper set the situational account against the newspaper explanations of the day, which blamed apathy, alienation and urban life. Whether a victim ends up helped is a separate question, because more witnesses means more people who might act, and the two questions have different answers.

origin.who: John M. Darley and Bibb Latané
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: The seizure experiment. Its first paragraph retells the New York Times account of the Kitty Genovese murder, citing Rosenthal's book, and its discussion likens the set-up to that case, where spectators knew others were watching but were kept by the walls between them from talking it over. The story the paper opens with has since been shown to be wrong on its central points, which is treated below and does not touch the experiment.

evidence: Fifty-nine female and thirteen male students in introductory psychology at New York University were contacted, and seventy of them supplied the data. They sat in separate rooms and talked over an intercom about problems of college life. One voice, prerecorded, mentioned a proneness to seizures, and later staged one. Only the victim's microphone was live during the fit, so the subject could not see the other listeners or tell what they were doing. The measure was the time from the start of the fit until she left her cubicle, where an assistant sat waiting at the end of the corridor. Two subjects saw through the fit and were dropped. Of those who thought they alone heard it, 85% reported the seizure before the victim's microphone cut off, against 62% in three-person groups and 31% in six-person groups. The time column of the paper's first table reads 52, 93 and 166 seconds, and is not labelled as a mean. The likelihood test gave a chi-square of 7.91, p < .02, and the analysis of variance on speed scores gave F = 8.09, p < .01. Everyone in the two-person condition eventually reported it, against 62% of the six-person condition. Composition mattered less than number. A female subject reported at 62% whether the other bystander was female or male, and all five told he was a premedical student from a hospital emergency ward reported, a cell of five the authors read as showing no detectable effect. Of 16 personality and background measures, only the size of the community the subject grew up in correlated with speed of helping, r = -.26, p < .05. Subjects who did not report were not calm. They had trembling hands and sweating palms, and asked whether the victim was all right.

replication.headline: Fischer and colleagues pooled 105 independent effect sizes from more than 7,700 participants and found the effect held, at g = -0.35 in a fixed effects model.
replication.detail: That 2011 meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin covers the literature from the 1960s to 2010, and takes 105 fully independent effect sizes from 53 articles. The pooled figure is g = -0.35, 95% CI [-0.40, -0.29], under fixed effects, and g = -0.33, 95% CI [-0.45, -0.22], under random effects. A trim and fill analysis imputed no studies and moved neither estimate. The effect sizes were heterogeneous, Q(104) = 266.29, p < .001, so the moderator table carries most of the argument. Two of its cells are not weakened effects but reversals. Where a perpetrator was present the pooled g was 0.24, and in potentially dangerous villain acts it was 0.29, both positive and both significant, meaning extra bystanders went with more helping rather than less. Where the cost of intervening was physical the effect fell to g = -0.06 and stopped being significant. Bystanders who knew one another gave g = -0.24 against g = -0.46 for strangers. The old category of bystanders themselves in danger was dropped from every moderator test, on four effect sizes and a g of -0.90. The authors also record that the last systematic review before theirs, published in 1981, was not a quantitative meta-analysis in the modern sense.

study.cite: Fischer, P., Krueger, J. I., Greitemeyer, T., Vogrincic, C., Kastenmüller, A., Frey, D., Heene, M., Wicher, M., & Kainbacher, M. (2011). The bystander-effect: A meta-analytic review on bystander intervention in dangerous and non-dangerous emergencies. Psychological Bulletin, 137(4), 517-537.

limits: The field evidence answers a different question and comes out the other way. Philpot, Liebst, Levine, Bernasco and Lindegaard coded 219 clips of real public conflicts caught on monitored surveillance cameras in Amsterdam, Cape Town and Lancaster. At least one bystander intervened in 90.9% of them, with an average of 3.76 interveners per clip and 16.29 bystanders present. The rate did not differ between the three countries, and a Bayes factor of 17.27 favoured no association with national context. More bystanders made help more likely rather than less: each additional one raised the odds that somebody intervened by a factor of 1.10, 95% CI [1.03, 1.18], p = .008. The authors list reasons the figure may be high, including a broad definition of intervention that counts a calming gesture, and a sample drawn from inner-city entertainment districts. They also state that their design does not test whether a single bystander is less likely to help when others are present, which is the effect itself. Danger points the same way in the field. Lindegaard and colleagues coded 80 conflicts in five-second intervals and found the odds of intervention about 19 times higher when aggression was present than when it was absent, though the three severity levels did not differ from each other. Latané and Nida's 1981 review is named here and was not obtained, and no figure is quoted from it. On 21 September 2026 the publisher's own record answered with an Imperva bot block rather than a paywall notice, ResearchGate served a captcha, and Crossref, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Internet Archive item search held no open copy. Fischer and colleagues' 2006 experiment on dangerous emergencies was not read either. The publisher answered with a Cloudflare interstitial on the same day, and the only open record indexed for it, a Figshare deposit of a submitted version, holds no file at all.
misreadings: The founding story is not evidence. Manning, Levine and Collins went through the trial transcripts from People v. Moseley and the associated legal documents, and found no support for the three features that textbooks repeat: that there were 38 witnesses, that they watched from their windows throughout, and that none of them acted. Five residents of the overlooking apartments were called at trial, and three of them were eyewitnesses who saw Genovese and Moseley together. None reported seeing the stabbing. One shouted from his window and frightened the attacker off, and Genovese then walked around the corner of the building, where the second and fatal attack happened in a stairwell out of sight. There were two attacks, not three, a correction the authors take from De May's archive work rather than from the trial record, and no list of the 38 has ever been produced. The three witnesses who testified all described a first glimpse that did not read as a murder. All ten of the popular textbooks the authors examined carry the story, seven of them in a box, subsection or picture. The second misreading runs the other way. A victim in a crowd is not thereby doomed, because the effect describes each witness separately, and the aggregate rate of getting help in real conflicts is around nine in ten. Darley and Latané had already noticed the arithmetic: by their own calculation a victim was about as likely to be helped by two bystanders as by one, and the deficit against five showed only in the first minute.
